title: Mice and Mystics - an overview / review
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ytt9pEb78FA

Daniel (@dungeondive) revisits Mice and Mystics, Jerry Hawthorne's now-venerable classic and the clear prototype for his later storybook games Stuffed Fables and Comanauts. What sets it apart, he argues, is atmosphere: a cohesive design and genuinely good prose (credited to the mysterious "Mr. Bistro") that teleport players into an autumn-tinged world of mice scurrying through castle tunnels. He frames it not as anthropomorphic pop-culture but as a beast epic in the lineage of Watership Down and Walter Wangerin's The Book of the Dun Cow, which he pauses to recommend warmly. Mechanically it's simple: characters roll dice for movement and combat, spend "cheese" as a currency to level up and fire off powers, and search a large, characterful item deck. An initiative-clock timer drives surges of enemies and keeps things moving. Daniel mounts a spirited defence of dice against modern designs that shun them — "cubes of drama" that manufacture tension craps-style — noting how Shut Up & Sit Down and others soured on the game for exactly that. He concedes fuzzy iconography and inelegant rules, but says theme and story more than compensate. A gorgeous gateway crawl, and one he predicts will become a HeroQuest-tier collectible.

----

Are dice "cubes of drama" that make a game sing, or randomness that undercuts skill? And which game first pulled a dice-skeptic in your life into the dungeon-crawl hobby?
